## What the law says

- **Circuit protection:** From 29 March 2023, all power outlets and lighting circuits must be connected to a switchboard-type circuit breaker that complies with AS/NZS 3000, and a switchboard-type residual current device (RCD) that complies with a listed standard [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). - **Duty to comply and maintain:** The landlord must ensure the premises comply with the rental minimum standards on or before the day you move in [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The landlord must also keep the premises in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Qualified repairers:** Any repairs or works must be done by a suitably qualified person [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations summary says only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, both urgent and non-urgent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Electrical safety checks:** The landlord must ensure an electrical safety check is done every 2 years by a licensed or registered electrician [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The landlord must give you the date of the most recent check in writing on request [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What you can ask for or do

1. **Written request for a repair:** Tell the landlord in writing as soon as practicable about damage or a breakdown of supplied facilities or equipment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Regulations summary says the landlord must carry out non-urgent repairs within a reasonable time, and you may apply to VCAT if they are not done within 14 days of notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **Urgent repair:** Urgent repairs include failure or breakdown of an essential service or appliance for heating or cooking supplied by the landlord [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Because the tripping affects heating and cooking, you may be able to treat it as urgent, but the documents don't list every urgent repair, so check the Consumer Affairs Victoria guidance they refer to [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If the premises don't meet the standards, you can issue a request for urgent repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **If the landlord doesn't act:** If you arrange urgent repairs yourself after reasonable steps, you may be reimbursed directly for reasonable costs up to $2,500. You may apply to VCAT if you can't meet the cost, the cost is more than $2,500, or the landlord refuses to pay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **Ask for the electrical safety records:** Request the date of the most recent electrical safety check in writing [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). - **Form requirements.** A notice to vacate is not valid unless it is in the prescribed form, addressed to you, signed, and states the reason(s) for the notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Tribunal considerations.** When deciding a possession order, VCAT must consider whether it is reasonable and proportionate, including "the behaviour of the residential rental provider" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal also cannot make a possession order unless the notice has not been withdrawn [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

1. **The stated reason and section number.** The notice must give specific details of the reason, not just a general statement [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

4. **Your written repair request.** Renters must give written notice of breakdowns "as soon as practicable" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Keep your written request and any proof it was sent or received.
5. **Documentary evidence.** For a repairs notice, check whether the required evidence was attached [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

The retrieved documents **do not specify a minimum number of power-point or electrical circuits** that a Victorian rental must have. Therefore, I cannot say that having most power points on one circuit is, by itself, unlawful.

However, from **29 March 2023**, all power outlets and lighting circuits in rented premises must be connected to a compliant switchboard-type circuit breaker and a compliant residual-current device (RCD). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The rental provider must maintain the premises in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation, and repairs must be performed by a suitably qualified person. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The provider must also arrange an electrical safety check of electrical installations, appliances and fittings provided by the provider every 2 years, and give you the date of the most recent check in writing if you request it. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can ask for or do

Write to the rental provider or agent explaining that the breaker trips when the kettle and heater operate together, and ask them to:

- arrange a **licensed or registered electrician** to inspect the circuit, switchboard, outlets and relevant appliances; [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- confirm whether the electrical installation is safe and compliant; [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- provide the **date of the most recent electrical safety check in writing**; [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- carry out any repairs or electrical work the electrician identifies as necessary. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

You can ask specifically whether an additional circuit or other upgrade is needed, but the retrieved documents do **not** establish an entitlement to a particular number of circuits or to an additional circuit.

Until it is inspected, avoid repeatedly resetting the breaker or operating the kettle and heater together. Do not carry out electrical work yourself: the documents require repairs to be done by a suitably qualified person. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If the provider does not address it, give written notice of the problem. The prescribed agreement says non-urgent repairs must be carried out within a reasonable time, and you may apply to VCAT if they have not been completed within **14 days** after notice. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) The documents do not establish that this particular tripping problem is automatically an “urgent repair”; urgent repairs expressly include failure or breakdown of an essential service or appliance supplied for heating or cooking. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

**Current documents applied:** *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, **Authorised Version v009**, dated **30 June 2026** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf); and *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version v115**, dated **13 October 2026**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The documents do **not** state a general rule making every notice to vacate invalid merely because it was issued after a repair request. However, a notice must be based on a permitted statutory reason. For example, a repairs/renovations notice is permitted only where the provider intends to repair, renovate or reconstruct, has obtained necessary permits and consents, and the work cannot properly be done while you remain. It must give at least **90 days’ notice**. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- A notice to vacate must use the prescribed form, identify the reason and relevant section, provide specific details, state the termination date, and include required documentary evidence where applicable. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The prescribed form is **Form 6** under the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 009**. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- If the notice is for repairs under section 91ZX, you may challenge its validity at VCAT within **30 days after the notice is given**. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Act does not provide a different repairs-notice period merely because your agreement is month to month. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The rental provider cannot personally force you out; possession must be dealt with through VCAT and a warrant. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What to check and ask

1. **Check the stated reason.** Is it actually a section 91ZX repairs/renovations notice, or does it allege damage, threats, rent arrears or another breach? Compare the allegation with what you did: reporting leaks is not, by itself, the same as causing damage or threatening anyone. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

2. **Check the notice’s validity.** Confirm that it is Form 6, addressed to you, signed, gives a termination date at least 90 days away if based on repairs, explains the specific work, and includes the required evidence—such as permits or consents where relevant. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The documents do not specify a separate retaliation test, but this material may be relevant when challenging whether the stated reason is genuine and valid. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

4. **Consider a VCAT challenge promptly.** If the notice relies on section 91ZX or another section listed in section 91ZZS, apply to VCAT within **30 days** of receiving it and challenge its validity. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The prescribed notice itself also says a renter may challenge a notice if they believe it was given because they tried to exercise their rights. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

5. **Continue pursuing the repairs lawfully.** For urgent repairs, after taking reasonable steps to arrange them, you may arrange the work if the provider or agent does not do it; if you cannot afford the work or it exceeds the prescribed amount, you may apply to VCAT, which must hear the application within **2 business days**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) For non-urgent repairs, if the provider has not repaired them within **14 days** after written notice, you may apply to the Director for an investigation or to VCAT for an order. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The current Victorian rental minimum standards do **not** contain any rule specifying a minimum number of electrical circuits a rental property must have, nor do they dictate how many power points must be on separate circuits [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Because the tenancy regulations do not set circuit limits, you cannot demand that your landlord rewire the property to add more circuits solely under these rules. However, you have the following rights regarding maintenance and safety:

If the frequent tripping indicates a faulty breaker, overloaded wiring, or another electrical fault that needs fixing, you can formally request these repairs.

### What the law says about electrical safety
Under the current rental minimum standards, all power outlets and lighting circuits in a rental property must be connected to two specific safety devices [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf):

The retrieved documents **do not contain any rule** specifying a minimum number of circuits for a rental property, nor do they regulate how many power points can be grouped onto a single circuit or dictate circuit loading limits. 

### What you can ask for
Because the regulations do not mandate a specific number of circuits, you cannot demand additional circuits solely under these minimum standards. However, you can take the following steps:
1. **Request maintenance:** Formally ask your landlord or agent to address the frequent tripping as a repair issue. Landlords are generally responsible for maintaining electrical systems in good working order.
2. **Verify compliance:** Ask if the existing switchboard and RCDs meet the AS/NZS standards listed above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If they do not, you can request an upgrade to bring the electrical safety up to the legal minimum standard [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

answer:
Based on the Victorian residential tenancy laws in force today:

**1. Can you fix it without telling the owner?**
No. Under the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (rt-regs-2021-v005), you are legally required to notify your rental provider in writing "as soon as practicable of— damage to the premises" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The regulations explicitly state that "Where damage occurs, the renter must notify the rental provider in writing" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Attempting to fix it secretly would breach this obligation and could complicate any future dispute over the condition of the property.

**2. Who can fix it and who pays?**
You cannot simply hire anyone for a quick fix. The law states that "Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs—both urgent and non-urgent" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 
Because the damage was caused by your dog (a failure to ensure care was taken to avoid damaging the premises), the property owner is not obligated to repair it themselves under the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (rta-1997-v090) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf). Instead, they can issue you a formal written repair notice requiring you to fix the skirting boards at your own expense within 14 days in a "tradesman-like manner" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf). If you do not complete the repairs properly within that timeframe, or if the owner chooses to handle it themselves, they are entitled to recover the "reasonable costs of repairs" from you [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf).

**3. Would it affect the owner's insurance?**
The provided legal documents do not contain any information regarding how tenant-caused damage affects a property owner's insurance policy. 

**What you should do next:**
- Notify your rental provider in writing immediately about the damage to the skirting boards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- Ask them if they would like you to arrange for a qualified tradesperson to repair it, or if they will handle the repairs and charge you for the reasonable costs [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf).
- Ensure that any repairs you do arrange are carried out by a "suitably qualified person" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

Yes, rooming house operators in Victoria are generally allowed to charge residents for using laundry facilities like coin-operated washing machines, but they must follow strict transparency and provision rules under current law.

### 📜 What the Law Says Today
**1. Charging for Services is Permitted (with conditions)**
Under the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026), operators are allowed to charge for services like laundry [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). However, if they do charge you:
* They must give you a **separate schedule of the service costs** *before* you move into your room [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* If you use the service, they must provide you with an **itemised account** showing your individual use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

*(Note: If your rooming house is managed by Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency, they can only impose a laundry service charge if it's impossible to accurately measure your use, and the charge cannot exceed the actual cost of providing the service [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).)*

**2. The Machine Must Be Provided & Maintained**
Under the *Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023* (Authorised Version No. 002, in force from 1 December 2024), operators are legally required to provide a washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). The law mandates the *provision* of the appliance, but does not explicitly state that it must be free.

### 🛠️ What You Can Do
* **Request Documentation:** If you haven't received a schedule of services with costs before moving in, or if you aren't getting itemised accounts for your laundry use, ask the operator to provide them immediately [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **Check the Cost:** Ensure the coin price reflects the actual cost of water and electricity. Excessive markups on utilities can sometimes be challenged as unreasonable.
* **Report Maintenance Issues:** If the machines are frequently broken or not "in good working order," you can raise a maintenance complaint with the operator. Persistent failure to maintain standards can be reported to Consumer Affairs Victoria.
* **Dispute Unfair Charges:** If you believe the charges are unfair, unreasonably high, or if the operator is failing to provide the required schedules/accounts, you can apply to VCAT (the Tribunal) for an order to vary or withdraw the charge [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). For personalised advice on your specific lease terms, contact Tenants Victoria.

*Disclaimer: This information is based on the current Victorian legislation retrieved and provided for educational purposes. It does not constitute formal legal advice.*

**The short answer:** The documents I found don't set a minimum number of circuits for a rental. They do set rules about how power outlets and lighting circuits must be protected, and they give you ways to get the problem fixed.

**What the law says**

- **Circuit protection:** From 29 March 2023, all power outlets and lighting circuits in rented premises must be connected to a switchboard-type circuit breaker that complies with AS/NZS 3000, and to a switchboard-type residual current device that meets one of the listed standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). This sets out the protective devices, not how many circuits there must be.
- **Duty to comply at move-in:** The rental provider must make sure the premises comply with the rental minimum standards on or before the day you move in [2, s 65A(1)].
- **Duty to maintain:** The provider must keep the premises in good repair and reasonably fit and suitable for occupation [2, s 68(1)].
- **Electrical safety checks:** Electrical installations and fittings the provider supplies must be checked every 2 years by a licensed or registered electrician [1, Sch 3 cl 1]. The provider must give you the date of the most recent check in writing if you ask [1, Sch 3 cl 1(1)].

**What you can ask for**

1. **An electrical safety check and its date.** You can request, in writing, the date of the most recent electrical safety check [1, Sch 3 cl 1(1)]. If no check has been done in the last 2 years, the provider must arrange one as soon as practicable [1, Sch 3 cl 1(2)].
2. **A repair.** Tripping breakers are a fault in the wiring or supply, so put the problem to the provider in writing. The renter must notify the provider in writing as soon as practicable of damage or a breakdown of facilities or equipment, and the provider must carry out non-urgent repairs within a reasonable time [3, Form 1 cl 26]. Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs [3, Form 1 cl 29; 2, s 68(4)]. The documents I found don't say whether a tripping breaker counts as an urgent repair. The urgent repairs list is on the Consumer Affairs Victoria website, which I can't check from these documents [3, Form 1 cl 30].
3. **VCAT if it isn't fixed.** For non-urgent repairs, you may apply to VCAT if the provider hasn't carried out the repairs within 14 days of receiving notice [3, Form 1 cl 26].

**What the documents don't cover**

- The minimum number of circuits, or whether kettles and heaters must be on separate circuits. The rooming house regulations require outlets in a rooming-house room, but they don't apply to a standard rental like yours .
- The rules for your specific electrical layout. For that, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria on 1300 558 181 [2, Form 24 (Part A, cl 7)].

**Versions used:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 is version 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 is version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Both are the latest versions in the documents, so both apply today (4 November 2026).

**Short answer:** The retrieved documents give you ways to challenge a notice to vacate, but they don't contain a clear general ban on retaliating against a repair request for a notice like yours. Some details are missing, as noted below.

**Documents relied on:** the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version (version) 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Form of notice:** A notice to vacate is not valid unless it is in the prescribed form, addressed to the renter, signed, states the reasons, and states the termination date [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Your stated grounds to challenge:** The prescribed form tells renters they may challenge a notice if they believe it was given "because you tried to exercise your rights as a renter," or if it was not given properly [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Time limit to challenge:** For notices given under sections 91ZX, 91ZY, 91ZZ, 91ZZA, 91ZZB or 91ZZC, a renter may apply to VCAT challenging validity within 30 days after the notice is given [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The retrieved text does not give a time limit for challenging other notices, though section 91ZZR preserves other rights to challenge [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Retaliation wording:** The only express "given in response to the exercise of a renter's right" rule in the excerpts applies to a notice under section 91ZK (threats and intimidation) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The excerpts do not show that it applies to a notice given after a repair request.
- **VCAT's power:** VCAT can decide whether the notice is valid. If it finds the notice valid, you generally cannot apply again unless exceptional circumstances exist [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Repairs:** You must give written notice of breakdowns or damage as soon as practicable [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). For non-urgent repairs, you may apply to VCAT if the landlord has not carried out repairs within 14 days after receiving written notice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What to check

1. **The stated reason and section number.** Is it a section listed in the 30-day challenge provision, such as 91ZX–91ZZC [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)? Is it a threats or intimidation notice under section 91ZK [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)?
2. **Form and content.** Is it on the prescribed form, signed, addressed to you, and specific about the reasons? If the reason requires documentary evidence, was it attached [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)?
3. **Dates.** Compare the date the notice was issued, the date it was sent, the delivery method, and the termination date. Check whether the termination date gives the minimum notice required for the reason given.
4. **Your repair requests.** Confirm whether your request was in writing and when you gave it. Keep copies and any timestamps.
5. **Whether the repairs are urgent.** The excerpts list urgent repairs only in general terms, such as failure of essential hot water, cooking, heating or laundry services [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The full definition is not in the retrieved text.

## What you can do or ask

- **Ask in writing** for the specific reason and any supporting documents.
- **Calendar the 30-day deadline** if the notice falls under sections 91ZX–91ZZC [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Act promptly for other notices, since the excerpts do not give a deadline for them.
- **Consider a repair application** if 14 days have passed since your written repair notice. Note that a non-urgent repair application can be affected by whether the repairs were needed because of your own acts or omissions [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Seek advice now.** The prescribed form advises contacting a community legal organisation listed on the Consumer Affairs Victoria website. It also gives consumer.vic.gov.au/renting and 1300 558 181 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **If the landlord applies for a possession order,** VCAT decides whether the landlord was entitled to give the notice. A landlord cannot personally use force to remove you. Only Victoria Police can do so under a VCAT warrant [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

- The full definitions in section 3 of the Act, including "urgent repairs."
- Any general anti-retaliation provision that covers repair requests.
- The time limit for challenging notices outside sections 91ZX–91ZZC.
- The minimum notice period for a month-to-month notice on your stated ground.

- The landlord must use the approved notice to vacate form, which tells you that if you don't leave by the date stated, the landlord may apply to VCAT for a possession order [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Asking formally may be an option, though the documents don't say whether a retrospective consent would fix the breach.

**What the law says**

- A renter must not intentionally or negligently cause damage to the rented premises, and damage does not include fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Chewing skirting boards is likely to count as damage, but the documents don't say how that applies to a dog.
- A renter who becomes aware of damage must give the provider written notice, as soon as practicable, of the fact that the damage occurred and its nature [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Notice can be given electronically under the Electronic Transactions (Victoria) Act 2000 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- If the provider gives a repair notice for damage caused by the renter's failure to take care, the renter has 14 days to repair it "in a proper and tradesman-like manner." If the renter doesn't, the provider may repair it at the renter's expense [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The renter must reimburse reasonable repair costs within 14 days after the provider gives written particulars of the cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- Renters must leave the premises, as far as practicable, in the same condition as when they moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

- **Telling the owner:** The law doesn't allow you to skip notice. You must tell the provider in writing as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Doing the repair first and not telling them would likely breach that duty.
- **Getting it fixed:** A suitably qualified person should do the work [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The owner can choose to have you repair it, or to do it and charge you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You could propose to the owner that you arrange a qualified tradesperson, and agree on the cost and timing in writing.
- **Urgent repair route:** The documents don't list skirting boards as urgent repairs. The examples given are hot water, cooking, heating, laundering, burst water services, gas leaks, and flood damage [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). - **The dog:** A renter may keep a pet only with the provider's written consent or a Tribunal order [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If you didn't get consent, the provider can apply to the Tribunal to exclude the pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You may want to check this too.
- **Moving out:** Give the written notice before you leave. At the end of the agreement, the provider or their agent must complete the final inspection and fill in the condition report within 10 days after the end date [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**What the law says**

- The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026) is the current version [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Its section 108 allows charges for electricity, gas and water in a separately metered room, but that section covers utilities, not laundry, and does not apply to shared rooms [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Section 109 requires an operator who charges for services to give the resident a separate schedule of the amounts before the resident takes up residency, and an itemised account of the resident's individual use if they use those services [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Section 109A lets Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency impose a service charge for laundry facilities in a declared rooming house, but only if it is not possible or practicable to measure the resident's use. The charge must not exceed the cost of providing the facility [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This section does not mention private operators.
- The Rooming House Standards require a washing machine for every 12 or fewer residents, from 26 February 2024. The standard does not say whether the machine must be free [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Check your paperwork.** Find out whether the charge appears in the schedule you were given before you moved in, as section 109 requires [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask for an itemised account.** If you are charged, the operator must give you an itemised account of your individual use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Find out who your operator is.** If Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency imposes the charge, it must give you written notice of the charge and its particulars [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You may apply to the Tribunal for an order to withdraw or vary it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Check the machines' condition.** The operator must provide the required laundry facilities in good working order [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf) and must comply with the prescribed standards for any facility or service it provides [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

The retrieved documents **do not specify a minimum number of separate electrical circuits** that a Victorian rental must have. They do require that, from **29 March 2023**, all power-outlet and lighting circuits be connected to a compliant switchboard circuit breaker and residual-current device (RCD), meeting the listed Australian Standards. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The rental provider must also arrange an **electrical safety check every 2 years** by a licensed or registered electrician. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) A record of that check must include the electrician’s details, date, results, required repairs and actions taken. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The documents do not say that a breaker tripping when a kettle and heater run together, by itself, proves a breach or requires a particular number of circuits. They also do not establish from these facts whether the problem is an **urgent repair**.

## What you can ask for or do

Write to the rental provider or agent and:

1. **Report the repeated breaker trips and request an inspection and repair by a suitably qualified person.** The provider must maintain the premises in good repair and ensure repairs are done by a suitably qualified person. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
2. **Request, in writing, the date of the most recent electrical safety check.** The provider must give you that date in writing on request. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
3. **Request a copy of the most recent electrical safety-check record.** It must be provided within **7 days** of your written request. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
4. Ask the electrician to assess whether the circuit, switchboard, outlets and electrical load are safe and compliant, and whether additional circuits or other works are needed. The documents do **not** give you a right to demand a particular number of circuits. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

If the provider does not carry out a **non-urgent repair within 14 days** after receiving written notice, you may apply to the Director to investigate; you may also apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring specified repairs. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) If the premises do not comply with the electrical rental minimum standard, you may request urgent repairs to bring them into compliance. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

**Current documents used:** *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version **009**, dated 30 June 2026, authored by Lavina Mandy [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf); and *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version **115**, dated 13 October 2026, authored by Barbara Hargreaves [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

The current document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026** (“*rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf*”). [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

You must report damage or a breakdown of fixtures supplied by the rental provider **in writing as soon as practicable**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) For non-urgent repairs, if the provider has not repaired the problem within **14 days** after receiving written notice, you may apply to the Director for an investigation or to VCAT for a repairs order. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Urgent repairs have a separate process, including applying to VCAT; the Act says an urgent-repairs application must be heard within **2 business days**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

A notice to vacate must be in the prescribed form, addressed to you, signed, state the reason, and specify the termination date. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The prescribed notice form also says that a renter may be able to challenge a notice if it was given because they tried to exercise their rights as a renter. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

However, the retrieved Act does **not** set out a general provision expressly declaring every notice retaliating against a repair request invalid. The specific invalidity rules retrieved apply to particular notices—for example, a notice under section 91ZK is ineffective if given in response to exercising a right under the Act. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The documents therefore do not establish from the facts given that your notice is invalid.

## What you should check and ask for

1. **Check the notice itself:**  
   - Is it the prescribed notice-to-vacate form?  
   - Is it addressed to you and signed?  
   - Does it state a specific legal reason and termination date?  
   - Does it include any documentary evidence required for the stated reason? [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

2. **Check whether the stated reason matches the law.** For example, a notice based on intended repairs or renovations requires necessary permits and consents, the work must require you to vacate, and the notice must give at least **90 days**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

3. **Preserve evidence of possible retaliation:** keep your repair requests, photographs, videos, emails, text messages, inspection reports, the notice, and the exact dates and times—especially the fact that the notice followed your repair request the same day. The retrieved documents do not prescribe this evidence list, but the notice form states that a renter may challenge a notice on the basis that it was given for trying to exercise renter rights. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

4. **Do not assume “month to month” makes the notice automatically valid or invalid.** Check the statutory reason and notice requirements rather than relying only on the periodic nature of the agreement. The retrieved documents do not provide a general rule allowing termination merely because the agreement is month to month.

5. **Consider challenging it at VCAT promptly.** The prescribed form says notices may be challenged where the renter believes they were given because they tried to exercise their rights, and it advises seeking advice immediately. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) For notices under sections 91ZX, 91ZY, 91ZZ, 91ZZA, 91ZZB or 91ZZC, the Act expressly allows a validity challenge within **30 days** after the notice is given. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

6. **Continue pursuing the repair separately**, using the written-notice and 14-day process for non-urgent repairs, or the urgent-repair/VCAT process if the leaking fixture qualifies as urgent. The retrieved documents do not say whether your particular leaking fixture is urgent, so that classification cannot be determined from them. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The documents do not provide a general retaliation application, compensation rule, or a specific deadline for challenging every type of retaliatory notice.

### What the law says

Under the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115 (in force 13 October 2026)**, a rental provider must not unreasonably refuse consent to keep a pet. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The provider is taken to have consented unless, within **14 days** after receiving the request, they apply to the Tribunal for an order that refusal is reasonable. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Because you sent the request **three weeks ago**, the agent’s refusal alone is not enough if the rental provider did not apply to the Tribunal within those 14 days. The documents do not say that an owner’s allergy, or how often the owner visits, automatically justifies refusal. The Tribunal may consider the pet, the character and nature of the premises, fixtures and fittings, whether another Act permits refusal, prescribed matters, and any other relevant matter. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The current standard rental agreement also states that the renter must seek consent and that the rental provider must not unreasonably refuse a pet request. This appears in the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009 (in force 30 June 2026)**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

### What you can do or ask

Ask the agent in writing whether the rental provider applied to the Tribunal under **section 71D within 14 days** of your request, and ask for the application details. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If no application was made within that period, you can state that section 71C(2) says the provider is taken to have consented. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) However, section 71A says a renter may keep the pet where the provider has consented in writing **or** the Tribunal has made an order permitting it, so the documents do not clearly explain the practical step to take where consent is only deemed. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If the provider did apply within 14 days, the Tribunal can decide whether refusal is reasonable and may either permit the pet or, if refusal is reasonable, order that consent is refused and exclude the pet. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

### Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs?
**No.** The retrieved documents do not contain any rule specifying a minimum number of electrical circuits or mandating that power points be distributed across multiple circuits. Victorian tenancy law does not require high-load appliances like kettles and heaters to be on separate circuits from power points. Frequent tripping in this scenario is typically due to normal circuit overload rather than a breach of tenancy regulations.

### What can you ask for?
While there is no rule about the *number* of circuits, the law does set strict standards for electrical *safety* and maintenance. You can ask your landlord for the following:

* **Compliant Safety Equipment:** Your landlord must ensure that all power outlets and lighting circuits are connected to a switchboard-type Circuit Breaker and a Residual Current Device (RCD) that comply with Australian/New Zealand safety standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If your breaker is outdated or non-compliant, you can ask your landlord to upgrade it.
* **Proof of an Electrical Safety Check:** Your landlord is legally required to have an electrical safety check of all installations and fittings conducted by a licensed electrician every 2 years [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You can ask your landlord to provide the date of the most recent check in writing [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If one hasn't been done in the last two years, you can request they arrange it as soon as practicable [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **Repairs for Faulty Equipment:** If the frequent tripping indicates a faulty breaker or unsafe wiring (rather than just an overload), this falls under your landlord's obligation to maintain the premises in good repair. You can submit a written request for repairs. If the issue poses an immediate danger, it may qualify as an urgent repair requiring immediate attention [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

*Note: If you suspect the electrical system is genuinely unsafe or non-compliant, requesting a licensed electrician's inspection through your landlord is the correct procedural step.*

Based on the Victorian residential tenancy laws currently in force today (November 4, 2026), here is what the law says about your situation and the steps you must take to remove the occupant:

### 🔹 The Law on Unauthorized Occupants
Under the current regulations, a renter **must not assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the premises without the rental provider's written consent** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Allowing a friend to move in without your knowledge or consent constitutes an unauthorized assignment or sub-letting of part of the property [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 

### 🔹 What You Have to Do
To legally remove them, you must follow this formal process:

1. **Issue a Formal Notice to Vacate**  
   You must provide a written *Notice to Vacate* (Form 6) specifying the reason for the notice and a termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). For an unauthorized assignment or sub-letting, the termination date must be **at least 14 days** after the notice is given [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The notice must include specific details explaining why it is being issued; VCAT may find a notice invalid if it lacks sufficient detail [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

2. **Apply to VCAT (If They Do Not Leave)**  
   If your friend does not vacate by the termination date, you must apply to the **Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT)** for a possession order requiring them to leave [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). You will be notified of a hearing date, and VCAT will decide whether it is reasonable and proportionate to make the order [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

3. **Do Not Use Force**  
   You cannot personally use force to remove them or change the locks. **Only Victoria Police** can carry out a forcible eviction, and only when acting on a VCAT order (a warrant for possession) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

- *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (Authorised Version No. v009), in force from June 30, 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

The provider must give you written notice of the charge and any changes [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This section does not apply to private operators.

- A notice to vacate is invalid unless it is in the relevant prescribed form, addressed to you, signed, states the reason, and states the termination date. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The prescribed Form 6 also requires the rental provider to give the relevant section number and specific details explaining why the notice was given; merely quoting a general reason is not enough. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- The Act expressly says a notice under **section 91ZK** has no effect if it was given in response to your exercise, or proposed exercise, of a right under the Act. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The retrieved Act does **not** state a general rule making every notice issued after a repair request automatically invalid. ## What to check and what you can do

1. **Check the notice’s stated section and reason.** If it relies on repairs, check the 90-day period, the specific explanation, and whether supporting documentary evidence—such as permits or consents—was attached where required. ### Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs?
**No.** The Victorian rental minimum standards do not specify a minimum number of electrical circuits a property must have [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

While there is no set number of circuits, all existing power outlets and lighting circuits in your rental must meet specific safety requirements [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). * A switchboard-type Residual Current Device (RCD) that complies with AS/NZS 3190, AS/NZS 61008.1, or AS/NZS 61009.1 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### What can you ask for?
* **Safety Compliance:** You can ask your landlord or agent to ensure the existing electrical installation meets these minimum safety standards (i.e., that the breakers and RCDs are compliant) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 
* **Electrician Inspection:** Since your breaker is tripping when high-draw appliances run together, it is functioning correctly as an overload protection device. You can ask the landlord to have a licensed electrician inspect the switchboard to ensure the wiring and breaker ratings are adequate for modern living.
* **Upgrades:** If you need more power capacity, you may request that additional circuits be installed or the main switchboard be upgraded. However, adding new circuits is generally considered a property *improvement* rather than a mandatory repair under tenancy laws, so the landlord is not automatically required to do this unless the current setup breaches the safety standards mentioned above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**Applicable Law & Document**
Based on today's date (4 November 2026), the relevant legislation is the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021**, Authorised Version **v009** (in force from 30 June 2026) [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**What the Law Says About Retaliatory Notices**
Under the current regulations, if you believe a Notice to Vacate was issued because you tried to exercise your rights as a renter (which includes following up on necessary repairs), you have explicit grounds to challenge it at the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). When deciding whether to grant a possession order, VCAT must be satisfied that making such an order is "reasonable and proportionate" [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**What You Should Check on Your Notice**
1. **The Stated Reason**: Look at the specific section on your Notice to Vacate (Form 6) where the rental provider has indicated the reason for the termination [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 
2. **Grounds for Challenge**: Confirm that the notice falls under the category of being given because you "tried to exercise your rights as a renter" or due to "unlawful discrimination" [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Procedural Correctness**: Check if the notice was given properly, ensuring there are no errors, omissions, or incorrect information in the form [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

Yes, under Victorian law, rooming house operators are generally allowed to charge residents for using coin-operated washing machines. 

### The Law Today (In Force as of 4 November 2026)
The current legislation governing this is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version v115)**, which came into force on 13 October 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

* **Charging for Services:** Section 109 of the Act explicitly permits rooming house operators to charge residents for services. If they do so, they are legally required to provide you with a separate schedule of those service amounts *before* you take up residency, and must provide an itemised account showing your individual use if you use the services [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **Laundry Facilities:** Section 109A specifically recognises "laundry ... services or facilities" as chargeable items (noting that service charges can be imposed if it is not possible to accurately measure a resident's use), provided the charge does not exceed the actual cost of providing the facility [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **Requirement to Provide Machines:** The **Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023 (Authorised Version v002)** mandates that rooming houses must provide at least one washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). While the regulations require the *provision* of the machine, they do not mandate that it be free to use.

### What You Can Do
1. **Verify your paperwork:** Ensure you received a separate schedule of service charges before you moved in, and that you are receiving itemised accounts for your laundry usage [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
2. **Check the cost cap (if applicable):** If your rooming house is operated by Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency, the charge cannot exceed the actual cost of providing the laundry facility [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Challenge unfair charges:** If you are in a Homes Victoria/registered housing agency property and believe the charge is excessive or improperly applied, you can apply to the Tribunal for an order to withdraw or vary the service charge [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). For private operators, if they failed to provide the legally required schedule of services or itemised accounts, you may have grounds to dispute the charges through VCAT.

This applies regardless of the rent paid or the age of the property [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The landlord must ensure the premises comply with the rental minimum standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**What you can ask for**
1. **Urgent repair:** Urgent repairs include failure or breakdown of an essential service or appliance provided for heating, cooking or hot water [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether a tripping circuit counts. The full list is on the Consumer Affairs Victoria website, which isn't in the retrieved material. The rental provider should be notified in writing [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Once notified, the provider must carry out urgent repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If you have taken reasonable steps to get them done and the provider hasn't acted, you may arrange the repairs and seek reimbursement of up to $2,500 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). You can apply to VCAT if the provider won't pay or the cost is above $2,500 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **Non-urgent repair:** Give written notice as soon as practicable. The provider must carry it out within a reasonable time, and you can apply to VCAT if it isn't done within 14 days of notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Electrical safety information:** On written request, the provider must give you the date of the most recent electrical safety check [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). A copy of the most recent check must be provided within 7 days of your written request [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Checks must be done every 2 years by a licensed or registered electrician, and if none has been done in the last 2 years when you move in, the provider must arrange one as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **Qualified repairers:** Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What you should not do:** You must not remove, deactivate or otherwise interfere with prescribed safety devices [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). A residual current device is one of those devices [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). So don't bypass the safety switch, even if it's inconvenient.

**Gaps in the documents**
- No minimum number of circuits or outlets per circuit is specified.
- Nothing says you can require a new circuit to be installed.
- The documents don't say whether repeated tripping is a breach of the standard. In practice, asking for an electrician to check the circuits and the load would be the sensible first step, but that is my suggestion, not something the documents require.

## What the law says

The retrieved documents **do not set a minimum number of power-point circuits** for a Victorian rental. The current standard instead says that, from **29 March 2023**, all power outlets and lighting circuits must be connected to a compliant switchboard-type circuit breaker and a compliant residual-current device (RCD). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

A breaker repeatedly tripping when ordinary appliances are used together may indicate an electrical fault, inadequate capacity, or another issue, but the documents do not say that this situation automatically requires the provider to install a particular number of circuits. The rental provider must maintain the premises in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition, and repairs must be done by a suitably qualified person. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The provider must also arrange an electrical safety check of all electrical installations, appliances and fittings they provide every two years, and must arrange one as soon as practicable if no check was conducted within the previous two years when you moved in. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can ask for or do

1. **Write to the rental provider or agent** describing the repeated tripping, which outlets and appliances are involved, and when it occurs. A renter must give written notice as soon as practicable after becoming aware of a breakdown of facilities, fixtures or equipment provided by the rental provider. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

2. **Ask for a suitably qualified electrician to investigate and rectify the problem**, rather than simply resetting the breaker or telling you not to use particular appliances. You can also ask in writing for the date of the most recent electrical safety check. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

3. **Ask for the most recent electrical safety-check record.** The provider must give you a copy within **7 days** of receiving your written request; the record must include the electrician’s name and licence or registration number, the date, results, repairs required and actions taken, and an AS/NZS 3019 report. 

4. If the issue is treated as a **non-urgent repair** and is not fixed within **14 days** after your written notice, you may apply to the Director to investigate. You may also apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring specified non-urgent repairs after giving notice and waiting 14 days. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The documents do not establish that you can demand installation of a specific number of separate circuits. You can ask for the electrical system to be professionally inspected and any defect, unsafe condition or inadequate installation to be repaired; whether that requires additional circuits is for the suitably qualified electrician to determine under the applicable electrical requirements. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

**Current documents used:** *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, **Authorised Version 009** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), and *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version 115** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

Based on the Victorian residential tenancy laws currently in force (as of November 2026), here is how your situation is addressed:

### 🔌 Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs?
**No.** The retrieved regulations do not specify a minimum number of electrical circuits a rental property must have, nor do they set limits on how many appliances can run on a single circuit. 

The law only mandates that **all existing power outlets and lighting circuits** must be connected to:
* A switchboard-type Circuit Breaker complying with AS/NZS 3000 (Electrical Installations) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
* A switchboard-type Residual Current Device (RCD) complying with specific safety standards (e.g., AS/NZS 3190 or AS/NZS 61008.1) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### 📝 What can you ask for?
While the law doesn't dictate circuit quantity, your landlord still has legal obligations regarding electrical functionality and safety. You can take the following steps:

**1. Request a Maintenance/Repair**
Your landlord has a strict duty to maintain the rented premises in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Constantly tripping breakers when using standard appliances indicates the electrical setup may be inadequate or faulty. You should formally request that they redistribute outlets across different circuits or upgrade the switchboard to resolve the overload [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**2. Request an Electrical Safety Check**
Your landlord is legally required to have all electrical installations, appliances, and fittings checked every 2 years by a licensed or registered electrician [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If you don't know when the last check was, you can ask for this inspection immediately. The results must be provided to you in writing within 7 days of your request [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**3. Escalate to VCAT (If they refuse)**
* **Non-urgent repair:** Tripping breakers on one circuit is typically treated as a non-urgent repair. You must notify your landlord in writing, and they must carry out the repairs within a reasonable time. If they do not act within 14 days of receiving your notice, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring them to fix it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
* **Urgent repair:** If the electrical fault causes a complete loss of power or affects essential services (like heating or cooking), it may be classified as an urgent repair. In that case, your landlord must act immediately, and you may be able to arrange the repair yourself and claim up to $2,500 in reimbursement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**💡 Practical Tip:** When contacting your agent or landlord, frame the request around their duty to maintain the property in a "fit condition for occupation" and ask for an immediate electrical safety inspection to identify if the switchboard needs upgrading or if outlets need to be redistributed across separate circuits.

When deciding if a refusal is reasonable, the Tribunal considers factors such as the type of pet, the character and nature of the rented premises, and any other matter the Tribunal considers relevant [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

Because you sent your request three weeks ago (21 days), the statutory 14-day deadline has passed.

Based on Victorian residential tenancy law, if you are the **tenant** who allowed a friend to move into your rental without permission, here is what the law requires and the steps you must take:

### 1. Your Legal Position
By allowing someone to occupy the premises without your rental provider’s (landlord/agent) written consent, you have likely breached your duties under the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Specifically:
* **Unauthorized Assignment/Sub-letting:** You must not assign or sub-let any part of the premises to another person without the rental provider's written consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 
* **Causing Interference:** Permitting an unauthorized occupant can also be viewed as interfering with the reasonable peace, comfort, or privacy of others, which is a breach of duty [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### 2. Steps to Get Them Out
* **Inform Your Agent/Landlord Immediately:** You must notify your rental provider that your friend is no longer staying there. If you continue to allow them to stay, the rental provider can issue you a Notice to Vacate for breach of duty [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
* **Formally Request They Leave:** Ask your friend to vacate the property by a specific date. 
* **Cooperate with the Eviction Process:** If they refuse to leave, you cannot handle it yourself. You must allow your rental provider to issue a formal Notice to Vacate to you citing the unauthorized occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 

### 3. Critical Restrictions (Do Not Do This)
* **No Self-Help Evictions:** You cannot personally use force, change locks, or cut off utilities to remove them. Under Victorian law, only Victoria Police can carry out a forcible eviction, and only when acting on a VCAT possession order (warrant for possession) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
* **Do Not Ignore the Breach:** Continuing to let them stay puts your own tenancy at serious risk. The rental provider may issue you a Notice to Vacate, which you can challenge at VCAT if you believe it was given improperly or due to discrimination, but you should seek legal advice immediately [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

*(Note: If you are actually the **landlord/owner** asking how to remove a tenant (your friend) from your property, you must follow the standard eviction process by issuing a formal Notice to Vacate through the appropriate VCAT forms and applying for a possession order if they do not leave.)*
