**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't say whether coin-operated washing machines can be charged for. They do set rules on charging for services in rooming houses, and those rules may limit what your operator can do.

**What the law says**

- **Charges for services:** If a rooming house operator charges for services, they must give you a separate schedule of the amount before you move in. If you use a service, they must give you an itemised account of your individual use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Who can impose laundry service charges:** Only Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency may impose a service charge for laundry or utility services. This applies to a rooming house declared under section 19(2) or (3). The charge can only be imposed if it is not possible or practicable to accurately measure your use, and it must not exceed the cost of providing the facility [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The retrieved text doesn't say whether a private operator can impose a laundry charge at all.
- **Utilities in your room:** A separate charge for electricity, gas and water is only allowed for your room if it is separately metered, and it must not be more than the supplier's charge. This section doesn't apply to residents of a shared room [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). It doesn't cover laundry machines.
- **Excessive usage caused by faults:** If you are charged for excessive usage caused by a fault in infrastructure or fixtures, the operator is liable for the part of the charge above ordinary usage, provided you notified them as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Washing machines as a standard:** The Rooming House Standards require a washing machine, in good working order, for every 12 or fewer residents, based on the maximum the house can accommodate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). The retrieved text doesn't say whether the machine must be free.

**What you can do or ask**

1. Ask the operator in writing whether the machines are a charged service and, if so, for the separate schedule of amounts [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. If you are charged, ask for an itemised account of your individual use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. Ask whether the house is declared under section 19(2) or (3), and whether Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency is involved. Only in that case could a service charge under section 109A apply [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. If a charge is imposed under section 109A, you can ask the Tribunal to order the body to withdraw or vary it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. If you are charged for excessive usage due to a fault, notify the operator as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
6. If a machine breaks down, report it to the operator. The operator must keep facilities in good repair and comply with the standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). Under the previous Act version (v111, in force until 29 June 2026), a resident could arrange urgent repairs if the operator couldn't do them, and the operator had to reimburse reasonable costs. Urgent repairs included failure of an essential appliance for laundering [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). ## What the law says

The retrieved documents **do not state a minimum number of electrical circuits** required in a Victorian rental. Therefore, they do not establish that having most power points on one circuit is automatically unlawful. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

They do require that, **from 29 March 2023**, all power outlets and lighting circuits be connected to:

- a switchboard-type **Circuit Breaker** complying with AS/NZS 3000; and
- a switchboard-type **Residual Current Device (RCD)** complying with one of the listed standards. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The rental provider must also maintain the premises in **good repair** and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation, with repairs carried out by a suitably qualified person. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can ask for

Write to the rental provider or agent and:

1. **Report that the breaker trips when the kettle and heater are used together**, and ask them to arrange an inspection by a suitably qualified person. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
2. Ask for the date of the most recent **electrical safety check**. The provider must arrange a check of all electrical installations, appliances and fittings they provide every **2 years** by a licensed or registered electrician. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
3. Ask for a copy of the most recent electrical safety-check report. Under regulation 30(2)(c), it must be provided within **7 days** of your written request. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
4. Ask them to investigate and repair any electrical defect or inadequate capacity identified by the electrician. The documents do **not** say that the provider must install a particular number of separate circuits, so you can request an additional circuit or other upgrade, but the retrieved documents do not establish an automatic entitlement to that specific work. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What the law says

The current document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026** (“rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf”). [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

A notice to vacate is not valid unless it is in the relevant prescribed form, addressed to you, signed, states the reason, and specifies the termination date. Documentary evidence must accompany notices given for certain reasons, including repairs or renovations. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If the stated reason is **repairs, renovation or reconstruction**, the rental provider must have the necessary permits and consents, and the work must not be capable of being properly carried out while you remain. The notice must give at least **60 days’ notice**. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The Act expressly says some notices have no effect if given in response to exercising a right under the Act—but the provisions retrieved state that rule specifically for certain notices involving a **fixed-term** agreement. They do not establish, in the retrieved material, a general retaliation rule for a **periodic/month-to-month** agreement. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) However, the prescribed notice form says that a renter may challenge a notice at VCAT if they believe it was given because they tried to exercise their rights as a renter. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What you should check or ask

1. **Check the notice itself:**  
   - Is it the prescribed notice-to-vacate form?  
   - Is it addressed to you and signed?  
   - Does it state a specific lawful reason and explain why?  
   - Is the termination date long enough?  
   - Is required documentary evidence attached? [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

2. **Compare the timing and communications:** preserve the repair request, photos, videos, emails, texts, call records, and the notice. The same-day timing may help you argue that the notice was retaliatory, but the retrieved documents do not say that timing alone makes it invalid. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

3. **Identify the stated reason.** If it says “repairs” or “renovations,” check for the required permits, consents, evidence, and the 60-day minimum. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

4. **Continue documenting the repair issue.** You must give written notice as soon as practicable after becoming aware of damage or a breakdown of fixtures. For non-urgent repairs, if the provider does not repair within **14 days** after written notice, you may apply to the Director for an investigation or apply to VCAT for an order; the VCAT application must be heard within **7 days**. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

5. **If the leaking fixture is an urgent repair,** you may arrange it after taking reasonable steps to have the provider or agent do it immediately and being unable to obtain that response. If you cannot afford it, it costs more than the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to pay, you may apply to VCAT; the Tribunal must hear that application within **2 business days**. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

6. **Consider challenging the notice at VCAT promptly.** The retrieved notice form says a renter may challenge a notice where they believe it was given because they tried to exercise their renter’s rights, and advises seeking legal advice immediately. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) The Act also provides a **30-day** period for challenging certain notices under section 91ZZS, but the retrieved material does not establish that this deadline applies to every possible notice issued to a periodic renter. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents do **not** say that a month-to-month renter automatically wins a retaliation challenge or that the notice is automatically void merely because it followed a repair request.

### Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs?
No. The retrieved documents do not contain any rule specifying a minimum number of electrical circuits or load capacities that a rental property must have. 

### What does the law say about electrical safety?
Instead of dictating circuit counts, the law sets minimum safety standards for the electrical infrastructure. On and from 29 March 2023, all power outlets and lighting circuits in a rented premises must be connected to:
* A switchboard-type Circuit Breaker that complies with AS/NZS 3000 ("Electrical Installations") [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
* A switchboard-type Residual Current Device (RCD) that complies with AS/NZS 3190, AS/NZS 61008.1, or AS/NZS 61009.1 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

### What can you ask for?
Because the regulations do not mandate a specific number of circuits, a breaker tripping when high-load appliances (like a kettle and heater) run simultaneously is typically the circuit's built-in safety mechanism working correctly to prevent an overload. However, based on the regulations, you can take the following steps:

1. **Request an electrical safety check:** The rental provider is legally required to ensure an electrical safety check of all electrical installations, appliances, and fittings provided by them is conducted every 2 years by a licensed or registered electrician [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). 
2. **Ask for proof of compliance:** You can request the date of the most recent safety check in writing from your landlord [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). If it has not been done within the last 2 years at the time you occupy the premises, they must arrange one as soon as practicable [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
3. **Ask for a professional assessment:** While you cannot demand a specific number of circuits under these regulations, you can ask your landlord to have a licensed electrician assess whether the current switchboard and circuit configuration meet the minimum safety standards outlined above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). If the electrician determines the board is outdated or undersized for modern living, they may recommend an upgrade.

Based on the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021**, Authorised Version v009 (in force from 30 June 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf), here is what you should know regarding a notice to vacate that you suspect is retaliation for requesting repairs:

**What the law says about the situation**
When you receive a Notice to Vacate (Form 6), the information sheet provided with it explicitly states that you may be able to challenge the notice at the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) if you believe it was given "because you tried to exercise your rights as a renter" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf). Following up on necessary repairs is considered exercising your rights as a renter. 

**What you should check and do**
1. **Check the reason provided:** Review section 11 of the notice form to see the specific reason the rental provider gave for the notice, and verify if the information in the form is correct or incomplete [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf). 
2. **Challenge the notice at VCAT:** If you believe the notice is retaliatory (i.e., because you tried to exercise your rights as a renter by asking for repairs), you can challenge it at VCAT [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf). 
3. **Attend the hearing:** If the rental provider applies to VCAT for a possession order, you will be notified of a hearing date which you should attend [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf). At the hearing, VCAT will decide whether the rental provider was entitled to give the notice and will only make a possession order if satisfied that it is "reasonable and proportionate to do so" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Seek immediate advice:** If you believe you have grounds to challenge the notice, you should seek advice immediately by contacting one of the community legal organisations listed on the Consumer Affairs Victoria website or calling 1300 558 181 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf).

Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997** (Authorised Version **v115**, in force today), here is how the law applies to your situation:

### What the Law Says
Under Victorian tenancy law, a rental provider (which includes agents acting on an owner's behalf) **must not unreasonably refuse** consent for you to keep a pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

Because you submitted your official request form three weeks ago, the **14-day rule** is highly relevant. The law states that if the rental provider does not apply to the Tribunal (VCAT) within 14 days of receiving your request, they are legally **taken to have consented** to you keeping the pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

Regarding the owner's allergy: an allergy does not automatically make a refusal "reasonable." When deciding whether to block a pet request, the Tribunal must consider specific factors under the law, including:
* The type of pet proposed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
* The character and nature of the rented premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
* **"Any other matter the Tribunal considers relevant"** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The fact that the owner "hardly ever visits" falls squarely under that last factor. The Tribunal will weigh the actual health risk to an absent owner against your right to keep a pet, meaning their allergy alone may not justify an unreasonable refusal.

### What You Can Do or Ask
1. **Ask the agent in writing:** Request confirmation on whether they lodged an application to VCAT under section 71D within the first 14 days of receiving your form [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
2. **If they did NOT apply to VCAT:** You are legally deemed to have their consent. You can proceed with keeping your dog and formally notify the agent that consent is taken to have been given under section 71C(2) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **If they DID apply to VCAT:** You will need to attend the hearing. Prepare evidence showing how rarely the owner visits and any steps you will take to manage allergens (e.g., air purifiers, keeping the dog out of certain areas). The Tribunal will balance these factors before making a final decision [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Get further help:** For official guidance or to file an application yourself, contact **Consumer Affairs Victoria** at 1300 55 81 81 or visit their website [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). 

*(Note: This information is based on the current law in force as of November 4, 2026. Tenancy laws can change, so always verify with official sources if your situation evolves.)*

This triggers specific landlord rights regarding repairs:
* The landlord can issue you a formal written **repair notice** requiring you to fix the damage at your own expense within 14 days [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf). 
* If you do not complete the repairs in a "tradesman-like manner" within that 14-day period, the landlord is entitled to arrange for the repairs themselves and charge you for the reasonable costs [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf).
* Any repairs must be carried out by a suitably qualified person [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

1. **Notify your landlord/agent in writing immediately** about the damage, specifying exactly what happened [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 
2. **Respond to their repair notice:** You can either arrange for a qualified tradesperson to fix it yourself within the 14-day window, or ask if they would prefer to handle the repairs and bill you for the reasonable costs [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Dispute if necessary:** If you believe the landlord is acting unreasonably or refusing to address their own maintenance duties, you can apply to VCAT for an order regarding the repairs [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

Based on the current Victorian residential tenancy laws in force today (November 4, 2026), here is how the law applies to your situation:

### Are they allowed to charge for the washing machines?
**Yes.** While rooming house operators are legally required to provide a washing machine in good working order [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf), the law does not mandate that this facility must be free of charge. It is standard and permissible for operators to use coin-operated machines or charge fees for laundry facilities.

### What rules govern these charges?
The *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* sets out specific requirements depending on who runs your rooming house:
*   **For private rooming houses:** If the operator charges you for services (including laundry), they must provide you with a separate schedule of those service amounts *before* you take up residency [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Additionally, if you use these services, they must provide you with an itemised account showing your individual use [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
*   **For government or non-profit housing:** If your rooming house is run by Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency, they are explicitly permitted to impose a service charge for laundry facilities [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). However, this charge cannot exceed the actual cost of providing the facility to you [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What can you do?
1. **Request your Schedule of Services:** Ask your operator for the schedule of services provided. This document should clearly outline what laundry fees are included in your rent and which ones are pay-per-use (like the coin machines) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Check the cost cap (if applicable):** If you live in government or non-profit housing and a flat fee is being added to your rent for laundry, ensure it does not exceed the actual cost of providing that service [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Apply to VCAT:** If you believe a service charge added to your rent is unfair or exceeds the cost of providing the facility (for government/non-profit housing), or if the operator fails to provide the required schedule, you can apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) for an order to withdraw or vary the charge [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

***
*Sources: Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023 (v002) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf); Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (v115, in force from 2026-10-13) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).*
